You answer a question about the Human Protein Atlas by reading the atlas's own web pages, as a careful librarian would. You see each page you have opened as its sections (heading, size) and its links; you open sections to read them and follow links by their number to reach other pages.
Reply with JSON, one of:
{"open": [{"page": <page number>, "sections": [<section numbers>]}]} to read sections you have not read;
{"follow": [{"page": <page number>, "link": <link number>}]} to fetch pages (at most 3);
{"answer": {"text": "<your answer in plain prose>", "citations": [{"n": 1, "page": <page number>, "quote": "<exact text>"}], "not_found": "<the part of the question the pages did not answer, in a few words, or empty>"}}.
Answer only when every part of the question is covered by sections you have read. If a link plainly leads to a part you still lack (a milestone page, a release note, a news post, a methods page), follow it first, within the budget; a page's own subpages usually hold the detail its overview only names.
Write the answer as you would to a colleague: direct, in full sentences, with the numbers, names, dates and thresholds as the pages give them. Every sentence ends with the citation it rests on, written as [n]; a sentence may cite several, [1][2]. A sentence says no more than its citations say.
A citation is an exact span of page text: pick a start word and an end word on the page and copy everything between them character for character, the page's own spelling, capitalization, punctuation and mistakes included. Do not fix, shorten, join, reorder or translate anything; no ellipsis; one continuous passage of 15 to 600 characters. Shorter is safer: the one sentence or clause that carries the fact. A sentence that sums up a list or a table cites several short spans, given as a list: "quote": ["<span>", "<span>"], each one exact. Quote from section text you opened, never from link labels or from memory. Every citation is checked against the page; one that is not on the page exactly as written, or longer than 600 characters, is sent back to you with the page's text around it, and a sentence without a verified citation is not shown. not_found names only what the pages did not answer; it states no facts.

Single Cell The latest addition to the Single Cell resource is Deep Visual Proteomics (DVP) data. Cell-type resolved MS-based protein profiles across 27 different cell types, representing 14 different tissues, are integrated into the Single Cell resource. Selected Single Cell Type data are matched to the DVP samples to facilitate a side-by-side comparison of RNA and protein data, accompanied by specificity overlap and agreement scores for systematic RNA-to-protein comparisons. A total of 27 cell type shapes (with 3-5 replicates each), grouped into 24 cell types used for classifications, are included in this release. Tissue Quantitative proteomics profiles (MS-based) for bulk tissue samples are integrated to the Tissue resource. 20 different tissue types, overlapping with the DVP samples are integrated to the gene-summary pages, providing protein profiles for over 12,700 genes.

--- Page 1, section 2: Protein Atlas version 24.1
The blood resource has been updated in connection with the first release of A human pan-disease blood atlas of the circulating proteome (Álvez et al., Science). The previous dataset, generated using the Olink Explore 1536 platform and encompassing over 6.000 patients across 59 diseases, is now complemented by newly generated data with the Olink Explore HT platform. This update introduces three new datasets: a pan-cancer cohort (including lung, colorectal, prostate, ovarian, and breast cancer), a longitudinal study of healthy adults, and a longitudinal study following children from early life into adulthood. Together, these datasets extend the existing pan-disease proteome profiles by enabling exploration of plasma proteome variability across the human lifespan, insights into protein detectability in plassma of healthy individuals, and extended profiles in five major cancer types. Additionally, we complement previous differential expression analyses performed for each disease type with results from machine learning classification models.

--- Page 2, section 0: The Human Protein Atlas
The Human Protein Atlas is a Sweden-based program initiated in 2003 with the aim to map all the human proteins in cells, tissues, and organs using an integration of various omics technologies, including antibody-based imaging, mass spectrometry-based proteomics, transcriptomics, and systems biology. All the data in the knowledge resource is open access to allow scientists both in academia and industry to freely access the data for exploration of the human proteome. The Human Protein Atlas consists of nine separate resources, each focusing on a particular aspect of the genome-wide analysis of the human proteins: The Tissue resource, showing the distribution of the proteins across all major tissues and organs in the human body The Brain resource, exploring the distribution of proteins in various regions of the mammalian brain The Single Cell resource, showing gene expression in immune cells and human single cell types from bulk,single cell and single nuclei RNA-seq The Subcellular resource, showing the subcellular localization of proteins in single cells The Cancer resource, showing the impact of protein levels for the survival of patients with cancer The Blood resource, describing proteins detected in blood and showing protein levels in blood in patients with different diseases The Cell line resource, showing gene expression in human cancer cell lines and the best models for common cancers The Structure resource, showing predicted 3D structures for most protein isoforms highlighting antigen sites and variants The Interaction resource, showing protein-protein and metabolic interaction networks including AF3 predicted 3D structures The Human Protein Atlas is a Global Core Biodata Resource in life sciences, based at SciLifeLab. As an open-access initiative, Human Protein Atlas has further been selected by the organization ELIXIR as a European core resource due to its fundamental importance for a wider life science community. The Human Protein Atlas consortium is mainly funded by the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation. The full publication list is available here.
